title: The fires that taught Upakosala
word: a teaching role in the house
hookLine: the teacher leaves without teaching, and the fires of the house speak up
carry: Brahman is joy, as wide as space
tomorrow: what does a father say when he doesn't know the answer?

lines: A STUDENT WHO TENDS THE FIRES.
cards: A kitchen late at night, lit only by the stove's small flame. The warmth on your hands, the faint hiss. Now a student in an old house, the one who tends its fires morning and evening.
His name is Upakosala. Other students finish and go home; he stays. Then his teacher leaves on a journey without teaching him, and the student stops eating.

teach.b: The Chandogya Upanishad answers: the house does. First the teacher's wife.
Before he leaves she speaks up for the student: he has served well and tended the fires; teach him. He goes anyway. So she turns to the student: eat.
Why won't you eat? He's too full of sorrow, he says. Then the fires themselves.
The household fires he has tended talk it over: this one has served us well; let's teach him. Breath is Brahman, they tell him. Ka, joy, is Brahman.
Kha, space, is Brahman. He's honest: breath he understands, joy and space he doesn't. So they explain: what is joy is space, and what is space is joy.
Many teachers read it this way: the joy that is Brahman isn't a small pleasure that comes and goes, and the space isn't empty; Brahman is joy as wide as space. Then each fire teaches its own part.

Hindu homes still honor fire, in the lamp at the shrine and the flame waved at aarti. When the teacher comes home, he looks at the student and says: your face shines like one who knows Brahman. Who taught you?
Here's the thread from three days ago. That teacher is Satyakama, the boy who told the truth at a door.
His own teacher once said those same words to him. Now he says them to his student, and then finishes the teaching himself.

how: Some Hindu homes keep a lamp or flame at the household shrine, and the evening aarti waves a flame before the deity; in the old Vedic house the student tended the teacher's sacred fires.

games.q: what does “a teaching role in the house” mean?
o: the formal title of the eldest person at home
teaching that passes among the people of a home
a rule that only priests may teach the young

games.q: who taught Upakosala. tap the pairs.
p: spoke up for him: teach him
joy and space, which are one
your face shines like one who knows

s: Upakosala's teacher taught him everything before leaving
he left without teaching him; the fires and the teacher's wife stepped in.
Upakosala admits he doesn't understand joy and space
breath he understands; ka and kha he doesn't, so the fires explain.
Satyakama says words to Upakosala that were once said to him
you shine like one who knows Brahman: his own teacher said it to him first.

games.q: the fires tell Upakosala: ka, joy, is Brahman; kha, space, is Brahman. he says he doesn't get joy and space. what do they tell him?
o: the two are one: joy as wide as space.
joy is for later; study space first.
only the teacher can explain that.
games.why: what is ka is kha, and what is kha is ka. many teachers read it as: Brahman's joy isn't small, and its space isn't empty.

practice: If you have a candle or a lamp you can safely light, light it; if not, rest your eyes on any small light near you. Watch it the whole sit: its edges, its color, the way it moves when you breathe out.
Let it be the thing in your house that teaches, for a while.

wordCard.voice: A teaching role in the house: in Upakosala's story it passes among the teacher's wife, the fires he tended, and the teacher himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kha, space; with ka, joy, the fires tell Upakosala the two are one Brahman.

carryVoice: For the road: Brahman is joy, as wide as space. The fires he tended taught him that.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 4.10.1–4.10.5 (Upakosala tends the fires in Satyakama's house; the others are sent home; the teacher's wife asks her husband to teach him; he leaves; the student will not eat, full of sorrow; the fires decide to teach him: breath is Brahman, ka is Brahman, kha is Brahman; ka and kha are one)
Chandogya Upanishad 4.11–4.15 (each fire teaches; Satyakama: your face shines like one who knows Brahman; who taught you?; he completes the teaching)
Chandogya Upanishad 4.9.2 (Satyakama's own teacher: you shine like one who knows Brahman)
